text: Day 1
Day 1 started with a phishing email.

Not a sophisticated one. A password reset notification that looked almost exactly like the ones your IT team sends. One person clicked it. One person typed their credentials into a page that looked like your login portal but wasn't.
That was all I needed.
Days 2-11
I watched.

I logged in every second or third day. Always during business hours. Always from an IP that looked like it belonged in your region. I studied the account I had taken - what time she logged in, what she accessed, how long her sessions ran. I made sure I looked exactly like her.
On Day 8 I found your internal wiki. Network diagrams. Tool lists. And a page titled "VPN Access for Remote Teams" that included the exact version of your VPN software.
That version had a known vulnerability. Patched eight months ago. You hadn't applied it.
I noted it and kept watching.
Day 14
I found a shared service account - created for an integration project, never decommissioned, password unchanged for two years. It had local admin rights on eleven internal servers.
I had those eleven servers by the end of the day.
I still had not triggered a single alert.
Days 15-38
I deployed a lightweight persistence tool that looked like a scheduled system task. It checked in every six hours. It gave me a way back in even if the original credentials got reset.

I spent three weeks mapping everything - customer data, financial records, executive communications, backup infrastructure, disaster recovery timelines. I found the crown jewels. I learned exactly how to reach them whenever I decided to.
I didn't rush. Rushing is how people like me get caught.
Day 47
I exfiltrated a compressed archive of financial records and customer data through an outbound HTTPS connection. It looked like normal web traffic. It took eleven minutes.
I closed my connections and left.
Your team detected the breach on Day 61. Fourteen days after I was already gone.
What Would Have Stopped Me.
The phishing click was not the problem. People click things. The problem was everything that happened after it went completely unnoticed.

Would have flagged me on Day 1. My login behaviour didn't match the account owner's established baseline: wrong session duration, different access cadence, subtle but entirely measurable. A continuous identity risk score would have surfaced that anomaly before I ever located the service account.

Would have caught me on Day 14. One service account accessing eleven servers in a single session is not human behaviour. Ghost account monitoring combined with automated behavioural fingerprinting would have identified the pattern and responded autonomously - no ticket raised, no queue, no five-day wait.
I had 47 days because your tools were looking for known threats.
I am not a known threat. I am a behavioural pattern.

"Confessions of a Hacker" is a fictional narrative series based on real attack techniques and documented breach patterns. All scenarios are composites. No real organisations or individuals are identified.
